questions.q: What are the three distinct time periods presented in the poem “Blood”?
questions.a: The three time periods are: (1) the poet’s childhood playing on the sands with her brother, (2) the great‑grandmother’s youth — her elephant rides, marriage to a prince, and early widowhood, and (3) the poet’s adulthood — the great‑grandmother’s death, the cremation, the poet’s departure to other towns, and her later haunted memories. A wrong answer (e.g., listing only two periods or confusing the great‑grandmother’s youth with the poet’s childhood) reveals that the student cannot track the poem’s temporal shifts.

questions.q: How does the poet use the great‑grandmother’s stories to structure the narrative?
questions.a: The great‑grandmother’s stories create a story‑within‑a‑story (an embedded flashback) that interrupts the childhood frame. They provide the family’s aristocratic past — the “oldest blood” — which stands in stark contrast to the crumbling house of the present. This nested structure allows the poet to juxtapose past grandeur with present decay without leaving the childhood memory. A wrong answer that treats the stories as mere background information misses the structural function of the embedded narrative.

questions.q: If you were to divide the poem into three structural parts based on narrative focus, what would they be and which stanzas belong to each?
questions.a: Part 1 (Exposition): Childhood scene and description of the decaying house (opening stanzas up to “She was really simple”). Part 2 (Rising Action/Embedded Narrative): Great‑grandmother’s stories of her youth, the elephant ride, the jewel box, her marriage and widowhood (stanzas from “Fed on God for years” to “A blood thin and clear and fine”). Part 3 (Climax & Resolution): Great‑grandmother’s death, cremation, poet’s departure, and the final haunted apology (stanzas from “Finally she lay dying” to the end). A wrong answer that lumps the death scene with the childhood section shows inability to segment the narrative arc.

questions.q: Analyze how the shift from the great‑grandmother’s voice to the poet’s adult voice in the final section changes the narrative perspective.
questions.a: The great‑grandmother’s voice is oral, proud, and sorrowful (“O it hurts me she cried”), delivering the family legend. The adult poet’s voice is internal, guilt‑ridden, and reflective (“I have let you down / Old house, I seek forgiveness”). This shift moves the narrative from external storytelling to internal monologue, emphasizing that the burden of heritage has passed to the poet. A wrong answer that does not distinguish the voices treats the poem as a single undifferentiated monologue.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the poem’s non‑linear narrative structure effectively conveys the theme of decay and legacy.
questions.a: Yes. The fragmented, non‑linear structure — jumping from childhood memory to great‑grandmother’s youth to adult reflection — mirrors the physical fragmentation of the house (cracked walls, fallen tiles) and the psychological fragmentation of the speaker. The juxtaposition of past splendour (“jewel box”, “brocade”, “elephant ride”) with present ruin (“rats”, “white ants”, “pyre”) is only possible because the structure places them side by side. A wrong answer that calls the structure “confusing” without linking the confusion to the theme misses the deliberate artistic choice.

questions.q: Write a brief narrative poem (4–6 lines) that uses a similar structure: a childhood memory, a story told by an elder, and a present reflection on loss.
questions.a: A strong response will show three clear time frames, a clear shift in voice (child → elder → adult), and a reflective tone in the final lines. Example: “We sat on the porch / Grandfather spoke of the monsoon that drowned the fields / Now the well is dry / I taste dust in the wind / And hear his voice in the rustling leaves.” A poor answer lacks distinct time shifts or a clear narrative progression.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Plot and narrative structure in a narrative poem refer to the sequence of events (plot) and the ______ framework the poet uses to present them (structure), including shifts in time, perspective, voice, and stanzaic division that shape the reader's experience of the story.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are reading “Blood” for the first time and feel disoriented by the jumps between the poet’s childhood, her great‑______’s stories of riding an elephant, and the adult poet hearing the house crumble from distant towns.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
